speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not plan to take very much time of the House on this bill but I do wish first to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) for their attempt to recognize again the regional disparities which exist in some areas of Canada. I also wish to congratulate them on trying to reduce unemployment through the incentive proposed in the bill before us.
For the benefit of members of the House and others I should like to say that one does not see too many arrangements which take the regional disparities in this country into consideration. However, under this bill, in the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe region of Quebec a $2 tax credit per job is offered.
One must look at what is the objective of creating these jobs. The employer must find a new type of work and employ a person for three months in order to qualify for a tax credit for up to nine months of assistance, and the new employee must be employed full time. This should encourage small businesses in Nova Scotia, and in South Western Nova in particular, to consider this new method of reducing unemployment in the fields of fishing within the 200-mile limit, in farming, forestry and tourism.
There are some questions which I hope will be answered with regard to employment in the fishing area in cases where the catch is not available for the full 40 hours in a week or for the full three months. I hope that the minister will answer some questions I will put to him during the debate on this bill later on regarding the case of an employer who wishes to hire people in the fishing industry. Will he have to hire them for a steady three months' period to benefit, or will he be able to extend that period in case fish are not running for a period during that time? I wonder how the legislation should be

January 26, 1978
Income Tax Act
interpreted in that respect. There are many areas in Nova Scotia and in other Atlantic provinces where people are unemployed for eight weeks and more and this tax credit will encourage small businesses in these areas to create new jobs for one or more people.
As I said, in South Western Nova in particular the fishing industry is expanding, and hopes for the future are great. The 200-mile limit has certainly contributed to this. The tax credit for the creation of jobs will provide an incentive to reduce unemployment. It parallels perhaps the investment tax credit which was granted in the past year to small businesses which amounts to 10 per cent in the Atlantic provinces and in the Gaspe. It is 7 per cent in other designated areas in Quebec, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, and 5 per cent in all other areas of Canada.
To return to the tax credit proposed in the bill before us, it will amount to $2 in the Atlantic area and in the Gaspe, to $1.75 in other designated areas in Quebec, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, and to $1.50 in all other areas. It is calculated after the total taxable income of the company benefiting has been reported for that year. It can credit up to nine months of the $2 per hour for the employed person. It covers up to a maximum of 40 hours each week for a period of nine months. The employer can use this tax credit over a period of five years, if he cannot use it up entirely in one taxation year.
Often opposition members indicate that the government has not been looking for a method to alleviate unemployment in the regions of high unemployment in Canada. In my constituency this year approximately $2.2 million is going toward Canada Works projects. It is creating employment in times of high unemployment.
It is nice for members opposite to boast about the employment situation in Alberta, but a lot of Albertans have not faced the tough times of the east. This income tax credit will help many Canadians, particularly many easterners. I have a lot of confidence in the future of the east. I see businesses starting or expanding from existing businesses, not only because of the 200-mile limit, but because of Canada's ability to find oil on the east coast in the future. If one looks at the North Sea and sees how many wells were dug in order to find oil there, one will realize that Canada has not done as much and has found gas.
I see advantages for the constituency of South Western Nova. In order to receive the $2 tax credit, a person must find full-time employment for three months. I question the three months in terms of the fishing industry. Perhaps fish do not realize they have to be around for three months at a time. This is something that may be answered later in the debate. The benefit to the small businessman will be up to nine months and, if he cannot use the entire tax credit, he can spread it over a period of five years.
I thank Your Honour for allowing me to talk about this further incentive by the federal government. It is designed to

aid in reducing high unemployment in some of the areas of Canada. The job experience and training program under the Department of Employment and Immigration is very new. Chambers of commerce and boards of trade have already taken this problem in hand in order to find out whether companies could use additional unemployed youth between the ages of 18 and 24. They have attempted to find businesses which require this age group, at the same time as creating jobs for the future and taking advantage of the 50 per cent being paid by Manpower.
In conclusion, this two-year program regarding tax credit can only benefit Nova Scotia and my constituency. I congratulate the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Employment and Immigration.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is obvious from the expedition with which this bill was greeted today that there is a disposition on the part of the House to pass this bill as quickly as possible.
Would it not have been better if the government had brought this bill on when we wanted it, that is, prior to the adjournment for Christmas? The earliest this bill can be implemented is March 1, 1978, which means whatever advantages are in this bill will be lost for now. We hope there will be advantages in terms of its ability to create jobs in the private sector. I believe the private sector is where the greatest potential for job creation exists. But the advantages will have been lost, in so far as the peak periods of unemployment are concerned, namely, the winter season.
If the government had agreed to bring on this bill prior to the adjournment for Christmas, which is what we requested, it would have been passed in all stages in one day. The possibility that we might get through this bill today exists, and hopefully we will. The fact that we are dealing with the bill as late as today itself represents a tragedy because we will lose the job creation advantage of the bill at a time when we need it most. To underline that fact, all we have to do is look at the December unemployment rate, and it is growing by leaps and
Income Tax Act
bounds. The official unemployment rate for December stood at an all-time high of 8.5 per cent.
I suppose the government and the minister will draw some consolation from the fact that the rate of unemployment in December went up by only one tenth of I per cent over the previous month. There is a failure to recognize the fact that we are dealing here with human beings who are unemployed, and not just with statistics. While the government may draw some consolation from the fact that the rate December over November went up by only one tenth of one per cent, that official tabulation represents 40,000 people added to the number of jobless. That means that 40,000 more Canadians are without jobs.
If we examine the December figures one startling thing which stands out and which causes me a great deal of concern-and reference was made to this today in the question period-is the fact that a growing proportion of the unemployed have been unemployed for three months or more, which means that unemployment insurance benefits for these unfortunate Canadians are expiring at the rate of about 10,000 per week or about 2,000 Canadians every working day, according to December figures. For these people unemployment becomes a real tragedy because they no longer have the relative luxury of unemployment insurance cheques. These people have to make the decision to go to their local welfare officers and to submit themselves to the humiliation of means tests. In my view that holds the potential for great social unrest.
The official figures from Statistics Canada show that 37 per cent of those looking for work in December were unemployed for longer than three months. Of those unemployed for longer than three months 35 per cent represent working males 24 years of age and over, obviously heads of families. However, that is the official rate. In real terms the figures are even more startling because we have an army of unemployed numbering
I.	271 million as opposed to the official figure of 840,000.
The real rate of unemployment in Newfoundland is 26.3 per cent, or 57,000 out of a work force of 217,000. In Prince Edward Island the real rate is 19.6 per cent, or 11,000 out of a work force of 56,000. In Nova Scotia the real rate is 16 per cent, or 57,000 out of a work force of 356,000. In New Brunswick the real rate is 20.9 per cent, or 62,000 out of a work force of 296,000. In Quebec the real rate is 14 per cent, or 408,000 out of a work force of 2.922 million. In Ontario the real rate is 9.4, per cent or 393,000 out of a work force of 4.193 million. In Manitoba the real rate is 8.2 per cent, or 39,000 out of a work force of 475,000. In Saskatchewan the real rate is 6.3 per cent, or 27,000 out of a work force of
432,000.	These are the prairie provinces where employment is supposed to be at its highest. In Alberta the real rate is 7.1 per cent, or 66,000 out of a work force of 934,000. In British Columbia the real rate is 12.4 per cent, representing 151,000 out of a work force of 1.222 million. As I have said, the total number is 1.271 million unemployed Canadians, representing
II.	4 per cent unemployment.

January 26, 1978
Income Tax Act
According to the latest figures available, a little more than half of these people are eligible for unemployment insurance. The rest of them have to fall back on provincial or municipal welfare rolls. That raises a larger problem-which I hope is being discussed today at the finance ministers' conference-of the additional burden this places on the poorer provinces, because most of the long-term unemployment in the country resides in the five eastern provinces, Quebec and the four Atlantic provinces, comprising considerably less than half the work force.
I believe 37 per cent of the work force in Canada resides in the five eastern provinces, yet almost 50 per cent of the total unemployed resides there. I hope that the finance ministers will address themselves to redressing this legitimate grievance of the poorer provinces. I hesitate to use the term "poorer provinces", but those provinces lack the capacity to meet this additional financial burden. I hope some way will be found, apart altogether from the Canada Assistance Plan under which the government boasts of the 50-cent dollar, whereby half of the welfare is paid by the Government of Canada. That represents 100 per cent for the provinces because they have to pay out 50 per cent, when heretofore they had to pay out nothing because unemployment insurance covered the situation. That is a problem of growing concern.
The whole matter of the consequences of long-term unemployment on the individual has not been fully addressed by this government. I know that the Minister of Employment and Immigration is a compassionate man. I know he has a great deal of humanity and compassion, but I do not think he fully appreciates and understands what it means to be unemployed for a long period of time. I know what it means to the statisticians at Statistics Canada. It means that if you are unemployed for a long period of time and out of sheer frustration have given up looking for a job, you are no longer counted as being unemployed. You are not reported. In other words, you become one of the hidden unemployed, part of the indivisible army of unemployed, one of those for whom nobody holds any hope.
There are shortcomings in this bill which will be pointed out as we get into clause by clause examination. This bill is the only thing the government has come up with. We have asked for a new budget. There has been no response to that legitimate suggestion. Only a new budget can really address the comprehensive nature of this problem, the effect of long-term unemployment on the poorer provinces in terms of their capacity to meet additional welfare payments and the human consequences which flow from the effects of long-term unemployment. Only a new budget can prevent the social consequences which will result.
Youth unemployment is growing by leaps and bounds, and that is a real tragedy. Again, according to official Statistics Canada figures for the month of December, 15 per cent of the unemployed in the month of December was between the ages of 15 and 24. Many of them are university graduates or graduates from technical and vocational training schools. They have diplomas but no job opportunities. What does it do to a

young Canadian who works hard to get his diploma when his country shows him absolutely nothing in the way of opportunity? I say that makes for cynicism of the worst kind.
When I addressed a graduating class of a technical college in my constituency last June I was struck by the large number of people there and asked the college president if such a turnout was the usual thing on a nice day. He replied that they rarely got a full complement out as in the normal course the students would be in the field, working at jobs in forestry, construction, or the technical area in which they had graduated. They were present that day because there were no jobs for them.
Unemployment in my part of the country is critical, Mr. Chairman. The best barometer of that is the construction industry where, of a total work force of 20,000 people, about 16,000 are unemployed.
There is a disposition on the part of the House to get this bill through so that it can be operative by March 1. I hope the government will not impose so many bureaucratic-I do not use the word in a derogatory sense-regulations as to make it difficult for people to take advantage of the bill. I think particularly of small businessmen who do not have the resources to deal with bureaucracy and paperwork.
The bill is being sponsored by the Minister of Finance, but its implication will be the responsibility of the Minister of Employment and Immigration. I am glad to see he is here to pilot the bill through committee in the absence of the Minister of Finance who is quite legitimately away attending the conference of ministers of finance. I must say, however, that I think it would be an edifying experience for those provincial ministers of finance to watch these committee proceedings. They are going to have some input into the way the bill is implemented by providing advice to the government. Obviously the government cannot operate in a vacuum but will have to deal with the provinces, so I think those ten ministers of finance would be well served if they could observe committee stage of this bill from the galleries. I think they should understand what we are trying to do here.
All too often in this House when we put in place measures designed to cope with emergency situations, we make them so difficult that middle and small businessmen cannot take advantage of them. They are defeated before they start because of the numerous regulations and paperwork that must be coped with. I should like to ask the minister to address himself to this question as we proceed through committee stage.
The government is spending an impressive amount of money on make-work projects, various tax incentives, and manpower training programs-about $2 billion at the present time. The situation is not improving, however, although these programs have been in place for some time. The Canada Works Program has been in effect for a couple of years. The Young Canada Works Program has had very little impact on youth unemployment and, of course, the various government job training
January 26, 1978

programs obviously can have but minimal impact. Why train people if there are no jobs at the end of the training period?
In my part of the country many people occupy places in vocational schools taking upgrading or training courses financed by the government, only to find at the end there are no jobs for them. Some look for ways to return to the vocational training schools to take other courses. When we consider that over $2 billion has been spent on programs to provide incentives through the Income Tax Act, job training programs, make-work programs, the Federal Labour Intensive Program and others, we wonder just how effective they are. Sometimes I suspect we make it too difficult for people to participate. That does not apply to the Canada Works Program, however, because that was put in place quickly, although because of the scope of the program the impact is minimal. I do not underrate the importance of the Canada Works Program or the Young Canada Works Program but in my province where 57,000 people are unemployed only 10 per cent will find jobs through the $20 million spent on this program.
It is important that we approach this problem as an emergency-one that is unprecedented since the great depression. Unless we do, many Canadians will be forced to the streets, to the welfare offices, and will have to give up on the system. I believe we allow that to happen to our peril. We must treat this situation for what it is. If we approach it as an emergency we will impose a minimum of regulations and bureaucracy in order to ensure that the program is in place, operative and, hopefully, effective, as quickly as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I have a number of concerns about this bill. I realize that the job involved must be one that would not have been possible without the incentive of the tax credit, but I wonder what is the standard. Is it something that had existed in the past and had folded, or must it be something entirely new to the company?
Perhaps I can go on to my other concern. I realize that the company must not be receiving any other assistance in the form of a subsidy at the federal, provincial, or municipal level, but how does it affect companies presently receiving DREE assistance? Are they to be excluded from the program? The press release states that in order to receive the $2 tax credit which will be given for up to nine months, the person must be employed full time for three months. What is the interpretation of full time? In an area like South Western Nova where there is a volatile industry such as fishing, there may only be two months of herring fishing at the beginning of the season and a month some time later. Can that three months' full time employment be interrupted? I know that full time means the opposite of interruption, but in terms of the fishing industry how will full time employment be defined?
I commend the minister for this new measure. We all hope that most of the people who will be hired under this program will be rehired at the end of the subsidy. Perhaps I could get

If not required the credit could be carried forward for up to five years against future federal income tax liabilities and it will count as taxable income. That will be of greatest benefit to small companies that pay lower corporate tax rates than major firms. Again, I think that is good. Is that the total taxable income of the company, or do you relate it to the income earned from that new employment?
It has been brought to my attention that perhaps there might be a difference there. I would think that it would have to be the total income tax owed by the company rather than just relating it to the job. Perhaps the minister could advise if this program could be combined with JET, job experience in training, or is that excluded because it is a federal program? I imagine that the JET program will be receiving a subsidy, so you would not have that.
To reiterate, I have asked for two answers. What is the meaning of full time employment in an area where there is fishing, and whether a company which is presently receiving assistance under DREE would be able to qualify for creation of employment. Do you relate that new employment to the existing DREE having received a subsidy, or are you allowed to go into that?

My father was unemployed. 1 know what the impact is on a family when that occurs, and I do have concern for that. This was at a time when there was no unemployment insurance and no welfare. Similarly, I have been in the same predicament myself of being laid off and being unemployed,

speechtext:
In answer to the hon. member for South Western Nova, if DREE assistance is given as an incentive to increase the capital cost there will be no impact whatsoever. This program in fact will be available.
In the event DREE assistance is given to help with jobs, then the full amount of the tax credit will be given under this particular program, but in so far as DREE is concerned they will be looking at the particular form to see what impact this would have on the kinds of incentives and the amounts of money that would be made available. So it will impact to some extent on DREE in that particular region, but not where the incentives are given to increase the capital cost aspect.
I believe the hon. member for South Western Nova asked whether a firm which cuts down on its employment could apply. I can best say that it is in looking at the employment base, that an employer can measure the increment to his work. In the case of seasonal work the employment base would be the level of employment during the equivalent period of one year earlier. If it is in the case of on-seasonal employment, then the base would be the average level of employment during the eight weeks preceding the application. In the case of employment in heavy capital goods or the construction industry where employment levels tend to fluctuate widely but not necessarily seasonally, the base would be the greater of that reflected by the approach taken in either one or the other of the examples given, so that whichever one works in the least interests of the employer, that is the one which would be made applicable.
With respect to the job experience training program, a credit will not be given to employment which already receives support under other federal, provincial or municipal job subsidy plans. Persons who have worked for the employer within the previous eight weeks will not be referred by the Canada

Employment Centres, so that the JET program, being a federal program, would not be applicable.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT PROGRAM
speechtext: I take it that with those two exceptions the minister referred to, anybody who is carrying on a business will be treated as eligible employers. "Eligible employment" is full time employment where the work week exceeds 35 hours, that will last for a minimum of three months and that pays an hourly wage at least as high as the credit. speechtext: In cases where the approved employer has qualified employees under this legislation but operates his business at a loss and the loss continues year after year, is there a time when he will lose the tax credit available to him under this legislation since, if he does not earn a profit or file a tax return in which there is a tax payable, he will not have a tax credit available to him in the long run?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT PROGRAM

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister if it might have been possible, when this bill was being drafted, to enlarge its scope. Penetang has a very high rate of unemployment, and Orillia, which is highly industrialized, has experienced the closing of one plant and many lay-offs. My point is: the minister could have included that largely industrialized area of approximately 210,000 people in the DREE program in order for those people to be covered, and in an attempt to help other industries in the area as well. Why was this not possible? Is it still possible to do this?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for his compliment. If this program works out and is successful, as the hon. minister has indicated, would it not be advantageous to include an area like Simcoe county which has so much industry?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, because we are embarking on a new program, even though all ideas and suggestions may not be accepted now, I am sure they will be looked at. monitoring program provide for a monthly report to parliament?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT PROGRAM

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Simcoe North I am not very happy to be told that this program will not be of as much benefit to the businessmen and the unemployed in my area-and I assume also in the minister's area-as it will be in some other parts of Canada. For the first time in quite a number of years we see a definite increase in the number of job hunters. They appear to be quite willing even to go out to work on farms and ranches, and that is quite a change.
I suggest to the minister that the best opportunity for employment in these circumstances at the moment is in rural areas. We are in the throes of a very severe winter, one which is exceedingly hard on range cattle. It seems that last year's severe drought all over southern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan has given way to this severe winter and we have more snow now than the total fall of the last two winters. I hasten to say that I am not complaining about the severe winter. It seems we must have a lot of snow in order to get rain next spring. But it has created a demand for workers in rural areas.

The minister suggested to me that Mr. Bullock of small business is in favour of this program. My understanding is that this is certainly not what he had in mind but rather a much larger proposal based on an increase in wages over the year.
I should like to make a comment regarding the bureaucracy involved in the program. I think it is a significant deterrent to small business. First of all, an employer wishing to participate in the job creation program must approach a Canada Manpower Centre with a proposal. This proposal must be approved by the centre. Then the employer cannot go and hire any person whom he wants to hire, although that person may have been unemployed for eight weeks. He can only employ workers sent to him by the Manpower centre or else he will not get a tax credit. Also, he must sign an affidavit that he will create new jobs which he would not have had the financial ability to

create without the program. Then, when he applies for the tax
credit, assuming he has reached agreement with the Manpower centre, he must use a special tax schedule so they will know he is involved.
I do not see how this system can be said to require minimal red tape or how it is likely to produce jobs. Small businessmen especially who would stand to gain most from the tax credit may be reluctant to entangle themselves in all this bureaucracy and to risk the threat of a jail sentence or a fine if they are judged to have lied. In fact, the net value of the tax credit is not that attractive, particularly when one remembers that employers will presumably hire workers in a soft market and in a weak competitive position. Furthermore, this program is designed to reduce the hard core unemployed who, as group unemployment officers will tell you, will be unemployed from year to year. I think it is only fair to say that while the program may be of some value in improving the situation of this group of people, from the employer's point of view these people are not highly productive workers. That is the comment that I wish to make about the program.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ESTABLISH EMPLOYMENT TAX CREDIT PROGRAM

I think that this program could have been a lot more bureaucratic. It is a very simple procedure. The employer calls up, gets the form, fills it out, signs it and fills out his income tax form. It strikes me as a comparatively simple procedure.

Mr. Chairman, all corporations and those individuals who carry on business are required to make tax instalments. Corporate instalments are due monthly and

individual instalments quarterly. Generally speaking, the instalments due are based on the lesser of: (a) an estimate of the current year's taxes; or (b) last year's taxes, referred to in the legislation as the instalment base. The instalment base has always been defined by regulation.
The effect of the amendments to the regulations will be to permit a taxpayer to reduce his instalments for the current year by the benefit he estimates he will derive from the employment tax credit program. Thus an employer can reduce his 1978 tax instalments by the benefit he estimates he will get from this program in his 1978 tax year. We believe this feature will provide immediate stimulus to the economy and improve the take-up rate under the program.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is a relieving technical amendment to the definition of the capital cost of depreciable property. This definition now requires the capital cost of depreciable property to be reduced by the amount of certain grants, subsidies or tax credits which the taxpayer is entitled to receive from governments. Since the amount of the investment tax credit claim reduces cost, it also reduces the amount of depreciation that may be claimed. This amendment was necessary because of the relationship between the investment tax credit and the new employment tax credit. The taxpayer may claim any portion of either or both, as the circumstances require. It will insure that the capital cost of depreciable property will continue to be reduced only by the amount of investment tax credit actually claimed, not by the amount a taxpayer could have claimed.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-COMMITTEE OF REVIEW-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PUBLIC HEARINGS
PUBLIC SERVICE-COMMITTEE OF REVIEW-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PUBLIC HEARINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 23 at page 2092 of Hansard I asked the following question of the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) concerning the special committee on the review of personnel management and the merit principle in the public service:
Will this committee hold public hearings? If so. when? Also, will MPs and others be given the opportunity to express their views?
I received an answer as follows:

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-COMMITTEE OF REVIEW-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PUBLIC HEARINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will have to verify the impression I have that it is not the intention to hold public hearings. I will make sure whether that is the correct situation.
I raise the matter tonight because I think it is extremely important that there be no misunderstanding concerning the procedures to be followed by this special committee of investigation. I hope we will have a further statement tonight.
To sketch the background a little, on February 4, 1977, the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council announced the appointment of this special committee. It was to consist of a representative of the employers, Mr. Bruce Brittain, who had held a position at the deputy minister level in the public service for some time; a representative of the employees, Mr. Davidge, a highly respected spokesman for the public service; and the chairman of the committee named in the first week of January this year, Mr. Guy D'Avignon.
The government did not exactly move with haste in this matter because a recommendation was made that such a committee of inquiry be appointed in the joint report of the committee of the Senate and House of Commons presented unanimously in January of 1976. That report recommended changes in the Public Service Staff Relations Act. But it pointed out very clearly that the changes that had to be made in the Public Service Staff Relations Act, while long overdue, would require consequential amendments to the Public Service Employment Act. The former chairman of the Public Service Commission, Mr. John Carson, had repeatedly requested that this inquiry take place. In a special audit conducted in 1973 and reported in the 1974 annual report of the Public Service Commission, something over 6,000 appointments were examined in detail. A substantial proportion of them, perhaps a third, indicated irregularities in the form of violations of the Public Service Employment Act and/or the regulations issued under that act.
Adjournment Debate
Those of us who have been following events in the public service have been very much concerned with what has evolved over the period. We go back to the reports of the Glassco commission, that commission of investigation into government itself named by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was the prime minister of Canada. The Glassco commission brought forward a philosophy, a theory, a basic development of government policy, which said the organization had been too bureaucratic, that the comptroller general of the treasury had exerted too great a control. The Public Service Commission had exerted too strong a control on hiring. The Glassco commission said that the deputy ministers should be managers, that they should manage and have freedom and they should take responsibility for their own decisions. The Glassco commission also recommended certain safeguards be implemented. One half of the Glassco recommendations were implemented. The deputy ministers were given a great deal of discretion, but the other half, the checks on their operations, were not placed where they should be.
The Auditor General pointed out the consequences of this in his report of 1976, which was a bit of a blockbuster, and the government has moved to correct the bad administration which has crept in on the financial side. Very substantial improvements have taken place there. On the side of employment and personnel administration, I submit there have been equally serious defects that have crept into the operation of the public service and have not yet been corrected.
Those of us who have followed events are very much concerned, for example, about delegated authority, the procedure under which deputy ministers are making appointments. Sometimes the appointments they have made, for instance doubledecking, when candidates were required to go to language school, were clearly made without full examination of the requirements of the merit principle.

We are very much concerned about the situation of temporary help and what has developed in a number of areas here. We are concerned about the application of a computerized system of selection of applications for posts and the abuses that have crept in as a result of those who have learned how to beat the computer; how to put the right codes on their files; how to get the candidate that was wanted when a search was made in a computer, someone with say, ten years of experience in the northern territories for administrative posts, and by some strange coincidence only one candidate's name emerged when the file was examined. This kind of abuse of the procedures has become something of a legend in the public service today.
As a member representing an Ottawa constituency, I am pleased to see on the other side the representative of a neigh-

bouring constituency, Grenville-Carleton, the House leader of the opposition. I am sure he concurs with me on this.
We are very much concerned as to how this committee is going to operate. Will it hold public hearings or will it not? If it is not going to hold public hearings, why will it not do so? If it is not going to hold public hearings, how is it going to get the necessary input of information from those who are not in the public service itself?

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-COMMITTEE OF REVIEW-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PUBLIC HEARINGS
speechtext:
As everybody knows, Mr, Speaker, last Monday the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) answered the question the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) had asked him concerning the special committee on the review of personnel management and the merit principle in the public service, when he said that he did not feel at the time that the special committee intended to hold public hearings, but that he would make sure whether that was the correct situation.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to convey to the hon. member and to the House the information I have obtained. I have learned that to provide a forum of free and open discussion, and obtain as much information as possible, the special committee did not intend to hold public hearings at the early stage of its work. It may, however, decide to do so later on. Moreover, the special committee would directly ask parliamentarians, representatives of civil service unions and other interested people to appear to make their views known. The public at large would be invited to do the same through advertising in the papers.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REASON CANADIAN DELEGATION IN INDONESIA TO DISCUSS POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN COAL MINING PROJECT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REASON CANADIAN DELEGATION IN INDONESIA TO DISCUSS POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN COAL MINING PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week or so before the Christmas recess I raised the question of the propriety of this country sending a trade delegation to Indonesia, hoping to participate in the development of a billion dollar coal mining project. At the time the minister promised to make some inquiries and reply to me.
In the last two days prior to Christmas we had the debate on external affairs. Again I alluded to the trade relationship with Indonesia because what was going on simultaneously was a remarkable contrast to the minister's response to conditions in South Africa as he saw them in the withdrawing of Canadian representatives from that nation.
Since then I have received a reply from the minister. He assures me that the coal mining operation in Indonesia, if and when it comes on for local use, probably will not compete with Canadian mines. I find that a little strange to believe, particularly when he goes on with a qualifier. If that development

proceeded, it would be remarkable if the government of Indonesia did not see to it that a great deal of that coal were exported. It could very possibly be in direct competition with Canada.
I do not at all see it beyond the scope of Japanese technology to raise lower grade coal to the point where it could serve good use. Of course, within this country we have a great deal of low grade thermal coal that we might profitably export in a few years' time. However, if a development like this proceeds, we would not be able to do that.
I represent an area of British Columbia with a history of coal mining. The initial industrial base in the province was based on Vancouver Island and in the southeast Kootenay riding that I represent. The coal mining industry virtually died. It saw extremely hard times. It made a remarkable comeback, particularly in the south Kootenay corner. At the moment the development of several promising prospects there is being delayed.
I would still raise the question whether it is in the best interests of Canada to so actively promote industry abroad that will be in direct competition with our Canadian industry when developed. I have a great suspicion that what we gain in the short range will be lost in the long range.
If we are going to be righteous about South Africa how can we actively and aggressively promote trade with Indonesia which has been the object of a report by Amnesty International highly critical of that country and placing it far beyond South Africa in terms of restrictions upon human rights and freedoms? The minister says that all the evidence available to him rules out any suspicion that Indonesia is making forced labour from political prisoner camps available for industrial or mining projects. From this I gather he has failed to read the report made on that country by Amnesty International. It is a lengthy document, one of pocketbook size, and nobody who reads it could reach such a conclusion. This report was produced by an organization which is held in high repute internationally, one whose censure of South Africa has been accepted by the government. I find it strange that an organization should be supported when it draws attention to a situation in one country, and totally ignored when it draws attention to a desperate situation in another, because it happens to suit our purpose, in this case to develop trade. It also happens that Indonesia is not the object of massive censure as is South Africa.
In the light of these considerations I can only conclude that this question has not been given the scrutiny and consideration it deserves either by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce or, certainly, by the Department of External Affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Dupras (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REASON CANADIAN DELEGATION IN INDONESIA TO DISCUSS POSSIBLE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN COAL MINING PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a mission visited Indonesia recently led by an assistant deputy minister and comprised of officials from the Department of Industry,
January 26, 1978

Trade and Commerce and members of the engineering consulting community. Its object was to support a consortium of three highly recognized Canadian consulting firms in its bid to win an engineering services contract, financed by the World Bank, to co-ordinate what is known as the Sumatra project. This project, whose value is conservatively estimated at $1 million, includes the development of a coal mine, rail transportation, port facilities and two 375 megawatt thermal power plants. The government of Indonesia has decided that indigenous coal would be used for power generation wherever feasible and has requested financial and technical assistance from the World Bank in implementing the project.
Faced with stiff competition from countries such as the U.S.A., the U.K., Japan, Germany and France it would be presumptuous for Canada to believe that this project would not be implemented if we did not participate. We feel that if Canada is successful in winning the engineering contract it will enhance our opportunities to participate in the tremendous supply of capital equipment and related services needed. The expertise and capital equipment available from Canada in the rail, material handling, marine and thermal power sectors makes this truly a project worth pursuing. In addition, the number of jobs which could be created through export sales would be significant.

subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON CONTRACTING OUT WORK TO PRIVATE OPERATORS
NORTHERN AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON CONTRACTING OUT WORK TO PRIVATE OPERATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the Christmas recess, on December 6, 1977, to be precise, I raised two questions with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner). They are related questions and they have to do with job opportunities, economic development and government policy in the Northwest Territories. I was asking about the government's plans to alleviate unemployment in the Northwest Territories and the government's position as to contracting out work to private operators in the Northwest Territories.
I was not completely satisfied with the minister's reply at that time. He mentioned he would look into these matters and report back. Since then the minister has had an opportunity to visit the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Indeed, I believe he has gone as far north as some parts of Alaska. So I hope that whoever is replying for the minister will have better answers than I received at the time I raised these questions.
With that in mind I should like to make a couple of brief remarks on economic development and job opportunities in the Northwest Territories. First, I believe the Northwest Territories are paying a large part of the bill for operating the Territories. I can think of a number of users of our resources up there, namely, oil companies, the mining industry and so on, that are exploiting the resources in the north. So I suggest that vast amounts of revenue go to government and pay for labour. There has been oil production at Norman Wells for some 35 or 40 years. There is the lead and zinc operation run
Adjournment Debate
by Cominco in Pine Point. There are two gold mines operating in Yellowknife, the Con and Giant Mines. There is silver coming from Echo Bay mines. There is the Tungsten mine on the Yukon-Northwest Territories border. There is a gas well and pipeline operating out of Pointed Mountain. There is the lead and zinc mine at Nanisivik on Baffin Island, and there are a number of other operations which pay taxes to the government. I refer to personal income tax, taxes and royalties on the fur industry, and business taxes.
So I have come to the conclusion that the Northwest Territories is paying its own way. I suggest this because of the sources of revenue which I just mentioned and the fact that there are only 43,000 people spread over that vast territory. Therefore, I think it is the responsibility of the government to put some investment into the north to provide more jobs and to provide for northern development in a way that people in that part of the country can accept.
I should like to make a couple of suggestions, if I may. First, however, I should like to congratulate the minister on his recent announcement that the government will be spending some $40 million to complete the Liard highway which will link Nelson, British Columbia with Liard and Fort Simpson.
I certainly hope the government will seriously consider adopting the policy which was announced some time ago by the previous minister of Indian affairs and northern development of giving people in the Northwest Territories preference for jobs. I hope the minister will consider this very seriously, not only with respect to the labour force but with respect to the contractors, the people who have equipment, so that they will put these people to work on the building of the highway from Nelson, B.C. to Liard and Fort Simpson in the Northwest Territories. This policy was in effect some years ago, not that far back in fact, in a project in which northern people had preference. There was on-the-job training and it was working very well. However, much more is needed and many ideas are required.
I believe the government must show some initiative. I have received ideas from my constituents which they have transmitted to me through letters and phone calls and during visits. They are very concerned that there is such high unemployment there. In December when I raised this question with the minister I mentioned that in the village where I come from there was at that time 72.2 per cent unemployment. That situation has not changed much.
I hope the government will move toward this idea of northern preference, looking at some other ideas such as the construction of an all-weather highway, gravel though it would be, from Fort McMurray, Alberta, to Fort Smith in the Northwest Territories. I met with the minister of highways for Alberta five or six weeks ago and he was very enthusiastic about such an idea. As a matter of fact, the government of Alberta has been considering this very seriously. I hope the federal government will get together with that province and pursue that idea as soon as possible.

It is also my hope that the government will consider seriously the construction of a bridge across the Mackenzie River at Fort Providence. This is another long-range program that could be initiated and spread over a number of years, thereby alleviating unemployment and would be a positive step in the area of economic development, especially for the western Arctic.
Other areas that require consideration are the tourist industry, the settlement of land claims, and a number of others. Another matter on which I place high priority-and I have mentioned this time and time again-is serious government consideration of the housing problems in the Northwest Territories. I hope it will alleviate the situation by-

speakeroldname: Miss Aideen Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON CONTRACTING OUT WORK TO PRIVATE OPERATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present levels of employment in the Northwest Territories and the expectation of rapid growth in the labour force in the coming years pose important challenges to both the government and the people of the north. In December officials of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the government of the Northwest Territories met with representatives from most communities of the Mackenzie valley to discuss ways of increasing employment in those communities. The ideas suggested for new employment by those communities are being followed up by officials.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) also intends to convene a conference on economic development in the Northwest Territories at which representatives of business, native associations and other interested organizations can exchange ideas on future directions for northern economic development for specific sectors.
While there is serious unemployment in the Northwest Territories, a great deal of employment has been created. For example, in the petroleum industry last year 802 northerners from 30 different settlements were employed. In the Mackenzie Delta alone, Beaufort Sea drilling resulted in employment
for 194 northerners. In the mining industry it has been a priority of the government of the Northwest Territories to increase native employment through the use of rotation schemes which have been worked out with local communities. There have been significant increases in native employment at the Con Rycon, Terra and Echo Bay mines because of this initiative.
There will also be significant opportunities for employment in road construction this year. Work on two contracts on the northern part of the Dempster highway will be beginning again in the next few weeks. These will provide job opportunities for people from Fort McPherson.
The hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) referred to the Liard highway. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development announced on January 20 that construction will begin immediately on the Liard highway between Fort Simpson and the British Columbia border. This project and the regional economic development initiatives which the road will make possible have the potential to create some hundreds of jobs.
Steps have also been taken to facilitate the private sector in its own employment-creating initiatives. For example, the government has improved the terms of the various loan funds operating in the Northwest Territories to assist business development. In addition, during the past year the Department of Regional Economic Expansion began offering its special ARDA program and a number of new small businesses have been created with special ARDA assistance. The government is also assisting two native associations in establishing development corporations in anticipation of future land claim settlements. Since there is much to be done to create new jobs, the government and the private sector have been active in exploring new opportunities.
